questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of a circle is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

Substituting the radius $r=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\pi \cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The graph consists of $4$ parts: the line segment for $x\in [-5,-2],$ the arc of the quarter circle for $x\in [-2,0]\,,$ the line segment for $x\in [0,\frac{5}{2}]\,,$ and the line segment for $x\in [\frac{5}{2},5]\,.$
Therefore, we can write the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-5}^{-2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-2}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{5/2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{3}}+{{{\int }_{5/2}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{4}}
$$

The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-5,-2].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot 2 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-2,0]\,.$ The corresponding region is a quarter circle. In part 1, we found the area of the circle as $A=4\pi .$ So we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{4}A \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 4\pi  \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [0,\frac{5}{2}]\,.$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The $4$th integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [\frac{5}{2},5]\,.$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}+(-{A}_{2})+(-{A}_{3})+{A}_{4} \\  & =3-\pi -\frac{5}{2}+\frac{5}{2} \\  & =3-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

From part $2,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x=3-\pi ,
$$

and from the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
{\int }_{-8}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-8}^{-5}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-5}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-8}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =\pi -3+3-\pi =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We split the integral into the sum of two integrals and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}({f}^{′}(x)-\sqrt{3})\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x-\sqrt{3}{\int }_{-1}^{0}\,\text{d}x \\  & =f(x)\,{|}_{-1}^{0}-\sqrt{3}x\,{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =(f(0)-f(-1))-\sqrt{3}(0-(-1)) \\  & =(-2-(-\sqrt{3}))-\sqrt{3} \\  & =-2+\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Using the quotient rule, we have 

$$
{lim}_{x\to 5/2}\,\frac{f(x)+{8}^{2x/5}}{{f}^{′}(x)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x-5)}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to 5/2}\,(f(x)+{8}^{2x/5})}{{lim}_{x\to 5/2}\,({f}^{′}(x)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x-5))}.
$$

We find from the graph that ${lim}_{x\to 5/2}\,f(x)=f(\frac{5}{2})=0$ and ${lim}_{x\to 5/2}\,{f}^{′}(x)={f}^{′}(\frac{5}{2})=\frac{4}{5}.$ Calculating the limits of the numerator and denominator separately, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} & {lim}_{x\to 5/2}\,(f(x)+{8}^{2x/5})=0+{8}^{1}=8, \\  & {lim}_{x\to 5/2}\,({f}^{′}(x)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x-5))=\frac{4}{5}-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡0=\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the quotient of these limits, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 5/2}\,\frac{f(x)+{8}^{2x/5}}{{f}^{′}(x)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x-5)} & =\frac{{lim}_{x\to 5/2}\,(f(x)+{8}^{2x/5})}{{lim}_{x\to 5/2}\,({f}^{′}(x)-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x-5))} \\  & =\frac{8}{(\frac{4}{5})} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Notice that, to calculate $g(-5),$ the lower and upper limits are the same. So, the integral evaluates to zero:

$$
g(-5)={\int }_{-5}^{-5}f(t)\,\text{d}t=0
$$

So, plugging in $x=-5$ gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -5}\,\frac{g(x)}{{x}^{2}+12x+35} & ={lim}_{x\to -5}\,\frac{{g}^{′}(x)}{[{x}^{2}+12x+35]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -5}\,\frac{{g}^{′}(x)}{2x+12} \\  & =\frac{{g}^{′}(-5)}{2\cdot (-5)+12} \\  & =\frac{f(-5)}{-10+12} \\  & =\frac{2}{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$
